An old emigrant points out a sheltered camp beyond the ridge.

events.text: A trace chain breaks while the team pulls through a washout.
A deserted sod chimney still shelters a little dry kindling.
A thunderclap scatters the oxen into the darkness.
At dawn, a neighbor leads two of your oxen back by their ropes.
Fine dust coats every cup and makes the youngest child cough.
A beaver dam has backed clear water into a willow bend.
A tin cup tumbles from the wagon and vanishes in the tall grass.
Spring ruts hold the wagon fast to its axles.
A Missouri farmer offers a sack of seed corn for a few cartridges.
Morning mist hides the far bank and every familiar landmark.
Wolves call beyond the firelight, keeping the camp awake.
A small creek has become a brown, rushing cut across the road.
A neighboring party begins a hymn as the evening settles.
Sage grouse rise suddenly from the brush beside the road.
Water drips from a loose hoop on one of the casks.
Cedar smoke from another camp drifts across the evening road.
Long days have raised raw blisters on a party member's heels.
A blackened strip of prairie offers a safe line before the wind shifts.
A cobbler traveling west can patch one pair of worn boots.
A gust extinguishes the cook fire before supper is ready.
Ants have found the sugar wrapped at the bottom of the provisions.
The wagon axle groans with every turn across the hard ground.
A bluejay steals bright scraps from the wash line at noon.
At Fort Laramie, a trapper warns of snow on the high road.
A cairn of white stones marks the safer bend described by the trapper.
A hailstone cracks a lantern globe just before nightfall.
Thimbleberries ripen along a damp northern slope.
A split rail blocks the trail where a ranch fence has fallen.
One ox stands apart with its head low and breath shallow.
A lean dog follows the train from an abandoned campsite.
A scrap of map paper blows from a passing rider's pocket.
The rider catches you at a ford and leaves dried apples in thanks.
A shallow pool is crowded with cattle from another wagon train.
A thorn branch tears a long seam in the wagon cover.
A marmot whistles from a rock pile above the trail.
Pine pitch has sealed a crack in a settler's spare water bucket.
Wet snow begins to gather on the wagon bows.
Clay under the wheels turns slick as soap.
A schoolteacher offers a book of Psalms for the evening fire.
Pale mushrooms stand in a meadow after two days of rain.
A bridge keeper demands coin to cross a narrow tributary cutting the road.
A Shoshone family shares news of a sheltered spring beyond the sage.
The sheltered spring is clear, with grass for the oxen and wild onions beside the bank.
A hard wind carries a favorite hat across the prairie.
Red spots appear on a child in a camp one hundred yards away.
A buried stump catches the rear wheel and cracks its rim.
A Pawnee trader offers a deer hide for a little coffee and cloth.
Frozen ruts jolt every spoke before the sun softens them.
Wild onions scent the low ground beside a creek.
The wagon tongue splits where it meets the yoke.
An abandoned mill offers a dry floor above the rain-soaked road.
All the fallen wood is green and hisses in the fire.
The sharp water at Soda Springs unsettles several stomachs.
A pack mule from another train noses around your grain sack.
The mule's owner finds you with a box of cartridges in gratitude.
A woman from a nearby camp shows you bitter roots that settle a stomach.
Granite chips scatter under the wheels in a narrow pass.
Cattle bells from a ranch carry over the plain at sundown.
The flour smells sour after a week of damp weather.
A tumbleweed catches beneath the brake and drags sparks over stone.
An emigrant widow offers a patched quilt for food enough to reach the fort.
At the next stop, the widow leaves a warm letter praising your help.
Ground squirrels have gnawed a hole through the grain sack.
A clear night has glazed the descent with black ice.
A small silver earring disappears while blankets are shaken out.
A Cayuse trader offers salmon for a small lot of trade goods.
The road narrows to a ledge above a rocky creek.
Sleet beats a cold rhythm on the canvas through the night.
A wagon rim is bent where yesterday's rock struck it.
Buffalo tracks have crossed the road until the wagon ruts disappear.
The tracks lead safely to a meadow with berries, grass for the oxen, and a clear creek.
Sun-warmed stones make a good place to mend clothes at noon.
Fresh earth beside the road marks a recent burial from another train.
Chokecherries hang dark and ripe along a creek bank.
Ice has formed at the edge of a stream you must cross.
A fort surgeon offers to examine the fevered member of your party.
A neighbor offers an extra ox for one difficult hill.
You return the borrowed ox with a handful of oats at the next camp.
A windfallen pine blocks the road through the timber.
A bedroll has soaked through where rain found a gap in the cover.
A line of river stones marks a safer place to water the animals.
A rein is frayed almost through near the bit.
The bacon burns while everyone argues over tomorrow's road.
A hand-dug well stands beside a lonely abandoned cabin.
The compass needle sticks against its cracked glass.
Coyotes have scattered a cache of dried meat left by someone else.
The water smells sharply of sulfur, though the animals drink eagerly.
A wheel wake in the mud points to a newer road around the hill.
The newer road reaches a firm, shallow ford before the evening rain.
A mountain goat watches from a shelf above the pass.
A spoon is missing after strangers shared your noon fire.
A bitter wind finds every gap in the wagon cover.
A fort blacksmith can reset a warped tire before the road worsens.
Ash from a distant grass fire dims the afternoon sun.
An ox has thrown a shoe on stony ground.
A widow at a trail cabin offers coffee and news of the road ahead.
A sudden gust overturns an open flour sack at supper.
The grass is cropped short where too many teams have camped.
A porcupine has chewed the leather lashings on a food chest.
A rare winter sun warms the camp at midday.
A peddler offers a sealed medicine kit beside the road.
The meadow grass hides a bog beneath the wagon path.
Lightning flashes beyond the hills without a drop of rain.
The last coffee grounds taste bitter, but wake the weary party.
A few loose planks offer a crossing over a muddy side channel.
A teacher gathers children from three wagons for an hour of lessons.
A carved cottonwood points west, but its arrow has weathered crooked.
A Mormon pioneer train shares a hymn at the edge of camp.
Packed snow narrows the Sierra road to one wagon width.
Tall reeds along the Humboldt hide a patch of good grazing.
White salt throws the noon sun into every eye.
A stone falls from Echo Canyon and dents the wagon side.
At Fort Walla Walla, a trader advises waiting for the river wind to ease.
Driftwood gathers along the Snake River bank after the storm.
Someone offers charcoal so each traveler may leave a name on Independence Rock.
A cool breeze at South Pass carries the first smell of pine.
A boatman at The Dalles offers news of a calm stretch below the rapids.
An orchard near the valley offers fallen apples after your long journey.
Cold rain blows sideways through the morning camp.
A wagonmaker asks to borrow your tools for an axle repair.
The wagonmaker returns your tools after the axle repair.

quotes.text: Mara Vail: Keep the kettle clean; sickness starts in small neglect.
Ephraim Cole: I count rivers by their sound, not their color.
Nell Grant: A child sleeps better when someone tells the truth about tomorrow.
Orson Pike: Never praise a shortcut until your wheels reach the other end.
Clara Wynn: I save one dry match for the morning after rain.
Jon Bell: The oxen forgive hard miles less quickly than people do.
Eliza Moss: A fair trade leaves both hands open.
Abel Finch: South Pass feels gentle only to those who have not climbed it.
Ruth Hale: We sing after supper so the homesick have company.
Micah Reed: A repaired strap deserves a second inspection.
Sarah Vance: I write down good water for the wagons behind us.
Caleb Ward: Weather is a neighbor that never asks permission.
Lydia Cross: Give grief a chair by the fire, then rise in the morning.
Thomas Quinn: The wagon tells you its trouble before it breaks.
Naomi Price: A full cup shared at dusk buys more peace than coin.
Gideon Marsh: The mountains keep no account of anyone's hurry.
Mercy Stone: A small kindness can carry a party through a bad day.
Isaac Turner: I trust a calm river less than a noisy one.
Hannah Fox: The prairie is wide enough to teach patience.
Josiah Wells: Let the weakest walker choose when camp is made.
Rebecca Hart: A fort's news is worth hearing twice from different mouths.
Daniel Shaw: We travel lighter after we forgive one another.
Ada Boone: Good boots are quiet wealth on this road.
Peter Lane: A clean bandage is better than a brave promise.
Abigail Frost: The last mile is easier when someone is waiting at camp.
Mara Vail: I scour the coffee pot with sand before breakfast; a greasy rim turns every cup sour.
Mara Vail: Put those cloths on the wagon rail. By noon the Kansas sun will dry them, or spoil them for good.
Mara Vail: I save bacon drippings in a corked jar; they mend a thin supper when flour is all we have.
Mara Vail: The pot stays on until it boils again. Let the drivers complain; the little ones are sick.
Mara Vail: I keep a pinch of tea for the person who cannot keep breakfast down; hot water alone feels like care.
Mara Vail: Green River will have our flour if we leave it loose. Eat the hard cakes now and spare the sack.
Mara Vail: I count beans into each pot instead of pouring from the sack; a careless hand can lose a week of meals.
Mara Vail: These apple peels came from our last barrel. Tonight they go in the oats, and nobody may call them scraps.
Mara Vail: I make broth from every bone after a hard day; tired people need salt more than fine cooking.
Mara Vail: Move that milk pail from the tent door. At Fort Kearney, flies arrive before the soldiers do.
Mara Vail: I wrap the bread in canvas, never loose paper; prairie dust finds every crack in a wagon.
Mara Vail: Hold your plate near the coals first. Porridge looks less fearsome when the tin is not frosted.
Mara Vail: I put the youngest child beside me at supper when grief is fresh; silence tastes less bitter there.
Mara Vail: Look at those hands. The dust has cut them worse than a knife; bring salt and warm water.
Mara Vail: I keep a covered cup for the driver; he forgets to drink until his voice turns thin.
Mara Vail: A mouse has found the meal sack. If you see flour on the boards, tell me before the mice invite cousins.
Mara Vail: I stir the pot slowly on windy evenings, because ashes in stew make everyone cross.
Mara Vail: Tomorrow we leave before daylight, so breakfast is already by the fire. Do not mistake it for supper.
Ephraim Cole: I test a ford with a pole upstream of the wagons; the quiet water often hides the deeper cut.
Ephraim Cole: See the cottonwood leaves turning downstream? Big Blue is rising, though the bank looks harmless yet.
Ephraim Cole: I never trust a pale line of stones under brown water; it may be a bar, or it may be a snag.
Ephraim Cole: Snake River turned a wagon sideways here last spring. Keep the tongue downstream and your people uphill.
Ephraim Cole: I mark a safe crossing with willow switches, then pull them when our train is through.
Ephraim Cole: You are thirsty, I know. Still, draw upstream of camp; horses and wash water have their own places.
Ephraim Cole: I listen for stones rolling beneath the current at night; that sound means the water is climbing.
Ephraim Cole: A shallow draw drowned a mule near Laramie once. Rain had fallen in hills none of us could see.
Ephraim Cole: I wet the wagon brakes before a steep riverbank; dry wood grabs too late when wheels begin to slide.
Ephraim Cole: Bare feet in the Kansas are a poor bargain. The riverbed keeps hooks, glass, and stones for fools.
Ephraim Cole: I fill every canteen before the road leaves a river, even when the next water is promised close.
Ephraim Cole: That foam caught in the grass is last night's water mark. Snake River was a different animal at dawn.
Ephraim Cole: I keep the children on the high bank until every ox is unyoked; a loose team is danger enough.
Ephraim Cole: Rope goes around the bolster, not the axle. I learned that after an axle spun a rescue rope into a noose.
Ephraim Cole: I taste the Humboldt only to spit it out; good water has no need to prove itself that way.
Ephraim Cole: Camp above the crossing tonight. By morning, twenty pairs of boots will have muddied the lower water.
Ephraim Cole: I would rather lose an afternoon than a wagon, and a river has never argued otherwise.
Nell Grant: Caleb says six times seven is forty-one. The wheels jolt his slate, but I suspect the road is innocent.
Nell Grant: I tell my boys the next hill is not a promise, only the next hill; that keeps them from counting miles aloud.
Nell Grant: Turn your coat collar over. I stitched your name there, though I hope no stranger ever needs to read it.
Nell Grant: I save my daughter's letters under the bedding; she writes to a grandmother who may never see them.
Nell Grant: No one is too small for kindling. The boys complain, then race back with twice what I asked for.
Nell Grant: I trade a story for a spoonful of medicine when fever makes a child refuse every remedy.
Nell Grant: Name three things you see, children: kettle, mule, moon. Now name one thing worse than this wind.
Nell Grant: I cut old shirts into strips for scraped knees, because grass does not care how fine a child's boots are.
Nell Grant: The eastbound rider waved back, so my youngest says Grandmother must be only two hills away.
Nell Grant: I keep a little flour for paste, so torn school pages may travel farther than their readers do.
Nell Grant: Make room in the middle. Annie sleeps there tonight; the Winter Quarters wind finds every edge of canvas.
Nell Grant: I do not hide a death from the children; I give them a task and let them say the name.
Nell Grant: We lost time today, not our manners. The hymn goes slowly, and the children still get their verse.
Nell Grant: I split one biscuit three ways if I must, but I never let the children see the empty flour sack.
Nell Grant: That doll is carrying seed corn, not a baby. We will plant it when the valley has a proper roof over us.
Nell Grant: I ask my son to read the trail signs aloud; a boy who reads a sign walks with his head up.
Nell Grant: Sunday means the blue ribbon, even in a wagon camp. Children need a day that does not look like Tuesday.
Orson Pike: I tap every wheel spoke with my knife handle; a dull answer tells me which one is loosening.
Orson Pike: Smell that? A hub is getting hot. Better grease it here than watch it smoke beyond Fort Kearney.
Orson Pike: I carry split hickory under the seat, for a wagon never breaks where there is a timber stand.
Orson Pike: Hear that new squeak? It is asking for grease, not an axle. Let us be polite while it is cheap.
Orson Pike: I use rawhide wet, then let it shrink around a cracked reach; it will hold until the next fort.
Orson Pike: Flour comes off before Blue Mountain's descent. A light wagon hears its brake better than a full one.
Orson Pike: I keep the spare wheel dry under canvas, because wet fellies swell and crack at the worst time.
Orson Pike: Put a rag between those irons tonight. The road shakes bolts loose without letting them chatter all night too.
Orson Pike: I mend a harness with square stitches, never long ones; long stitches tear like paper under a team.
Orson Pike: Everybody checks the wheels after Snake River. I check the kingbolt, where the mud hides its mischief.
Orson Pike: I keep a wedge beside the brake; one crooked wheel can make a camp of the whole train.
Orson Pike: That canvas patch was once a flour sack. The boot was wired shut at Fort Hall and still walks.
Orson Pike: I put the heavy tools low and forward; a wagon that topples teaches no useful lesson.
Orson Pike: Set the brake shoe before the Sierra storm comes. Wet ground gives a rolling wagon no manners.
Orson Pike: I ask for payment in nails before coins; nails are the only money a broken wagon accepts.
Orson Pike: Do not throw that harness away. The leather is done, but those buckles will outlive three more straps.
Orson Pike: I can make a wheel run crooked for ten miles, but I cannot make it safe; those are different jobs.
Orson Pike: Tallow the saw before that green wood. Otherwise the blade sticks and I say things children should not hear.
Clara Wynn: I keep my mother's thimble in my apron pocket, though I use a rougher one for wagon mending.
Clara Wynn: Shake that blanket farther from the fire. We have enough prairie in camp without breathing another garden bed.
Clara Wynn: I pin the wash to the wagon bows when rain threatens, so the wind does half the drying.
Clara Wynn: Who has only one sock? Speak now. By noon that missing one becomes a blister and then my work.
Clara Wynn: I fold the best quilt inward when we cross water, because memories weigh more when they are soaked.
Clara Wynn: Onion skins make a good dye. A patched sleeve need not announce itself from the next wagon.
Clara Wynn: I put dry grass under the bedrolls, so the cold ground does not climb into our bones.
Clara Wynn: This blue scrap is for Annie's doll. A gray camp can spare one bright thing, can it not?
Clara Wynn: I wash a cut with cooled tea when no clean water is near; it stings, but dirt stings longer.
Clara Wynn: We leave Fort Hall late if we must. These bedrolls stay out until the damp leaves them.
Clara Wynn: I keep the family Bible wrapped in oilcloth, beside the sewing needles and nowhere near the flour.
Clara Wynn: No, I will not trade the ribbon for coffee. We have coffee, and I am keeping one useless pretty thing.
Clara Wynn: I save the candle ends for storm nights, when a little light keeps the tent from feeling like a grave.
Clara Wynn: Mind the stone, it is warm. Tuck it by your feet and do not tell your brother it is better than his.
Clara Wynn: I keep spare laces in my hatband, because a good boot is useless with its tongue flapping open.
Clara Wynn: Mrs. Hale lent us two spoons and a pan at Walla Walla. I wrote it down, lest kindness become a quarrel.
Clara Wynn: I lay out tomorrow's clothes before dark, because hurried hands forget mittens and medicine alike.
Clara Wynn: Ox bells do not wake me now. A child saying home in the dark still does, even here near Willamette.
Jon Bell: I water the oxen before I drink, because they pull the water wagon as well as the load.
Jon Bell: Hold the lantern low. There is a pebble between his toes, and that pebble thinks it owns three days.
Jon Bell: I never yoke a sore ox beside the strongest one; the strong fellow will pull him lame.
Jon Bell: The captain wants miles; these collars want loosening. I know which complaint will still matter tomorrow.
Jon Bell: I carry bran for the weak ox, not as a treat but as a reason for him to rise again.
Jon Bell: Take the team wide of that badger hole. One broken leg can turn a wagon into a firewood pile by moonlight.
Jon Bell: I rub a mule's ears when flies are thick; a bothered mule saves his temper for the harness.
Jon Bell: Hobble them where they can see the fire. Even a steady ox imagines better grass when the dark comes.
Jon Bell: I keep a bell on the lead ox and a hand on its rope at riverbanks; livestock likes a bad idea first.
Jon Bell: Give them grain before the Sierra climb. Grass does not carry a mountain, and neither does wishing.
Jon Bell: I watch the oxen noses in dust storms; when they turn away, I know it is time to make camp.
Jon Bell: The hoof pick around my neck looks foolish until the one in the tool chest is half a mile behind us.
Jon Bell: I do not whip a frightened ox at a crossing; I let the calm one show him where to put his feet.
Jon Bell: Leave the best grass for the milk cow. Empty pails make hungry children louder than a whole team.
Jon Bell: I walk beside a tired team after supper, just to hear if any one of them favors a leg.
Jon Bell: The yokes sleep under canvas tonight. Wet wood will rub a neck raw before noon tomorrow.
Jon Bell: I have buried an ox and paid for another, and I would rather buy feed than repeat that lesson.
Eliza Moss: Mr. Dyer gave us two pounds of salt for cloth. There it is in the ledger; friendly does not mean forgotten.
Eliza Moss: I ask to see flour before I offer coffee; a clean sack tells more than a cheerful seller.
Eliza Moss: Needles, salt, and tobacco travel in separate packets. At Bridger, each starts a different kind of talk.
Eliza Moss: I never spend the last silver coin on a pretty thing, however much the road has made me want it.
Eliza Moss: Coffee is for trade before Green River, not after. Another wagon can carry dry goods better than ours can swim.
Eliza Moss: I count cartridges twice, once for hunting and once for trouble; the two piles must not meet.
Eliza Moss: That red blanket is handsome, but show me the weave. Color does not keep a sleeper warm at Winter Quarters.
Eliza Moss: I save my smallest coins for ferrymen, because a man at a river seldom has change.
Eliza Moss: Ask the Fort Boise clerk what sold out first. Travelers boast; empty shelves do not.
Eliza Moss: I will barter a spare dress for quinine without regret; fine cloth cannot cool a fever.
Eliza Moss: I have coin sewn into my petticoat for seed. A new farm begins before the first furrow, I suppose.
Eliza Moss: I pay a fair price for a map and then compare it with two others before I trust the ink.
Eliza Moss: No trading from an open wagon in this dust. Half the buyers only want shelter and the rest cannot see the goods.
Eliza Moss: I would rather have five sound needles than a pocket full of paper promises.
Eliza Moss: Salt costs less than spoiled meat. I buy it whenever Fort Laramie has it and the hungry look doubtful.
Eliza Moss: I keep trade cloth clean and folded; a rumpled bolt makes even good wool look doubtful.
Eliza Moss: Take my pencil, not my ledger. A debt without a mark waits quietly until it becomes a quarrel.
Eliza Moss: I measure wealth by useful things after supper: dry shoes, a full kettle, and a sound team.
Abel Finch: Take the south face where it is open. The north side keeps snow longer and its ground stays hard.
Abel Finch: I read wagon ruts for news: deep ones mean rain, wandering ones mean trouble ahead.
Abel Finch: The man calls it a shortcut. Has he walked it in rain? No? Then it is only a story near Bridger.
Abel Finch: I watch birds lift from grass before a storm; they know a low place before the wheels do.
Abel Finch: My compass lives in a wool sock. Laugh if you wish; a loose needle has sent families the wrong way.
Abel Finch: I mark bad water in charcoal on the map, then rub it out only after I have seen it twice.
Abel Finch: In this Blue Mountain fog, keep the wagon ahead in sight. Lose the road if you must, not your neighbors.
Abel Finch: I look for willow and cottonwood before I promise firewood; a green valley can still be bare.
Abel Finch: The water walk is longer from that high camp. It is shorter than wading from a flooded tent at dawn.
Abel Finch: I have seen fine weather close a mountain pass by sundown, so I keep a day of food uncounted.
Abel Finch: These fresh tracks leave Echo Canyon, but the old trail shows grass in its ruts. Tired people make poor guides.
Abel Finch: I put a white rag on thorn branches where the road divides, then fetch it when the last wagon passes.
Abel Finch: We are late, but we wait for sunrise. Guessing east across this desert can make a day disappear.
Abel Finch: I look for horse tracks near a fort, but I ask whose they are before I follow them.
Abel Finch: Your map says road. The ground says washout. Give the ground the last word.
Abel Finch: I note every spring that runs in August, because those are the ones worth seeking in a dry year.
Abel Finch: The short road is dust and the long one has grass. Look at those ribs; I know which road the oxen choose.
Ruth Hale: I start a hymn while I wash bandages; hands work steadier when the tent is not quiet.
Ruth Hale: The willow bark is in the paper twist. Take it with water, then sleep if the camp permits you.
Ruth Hale: I ask the grieving to carry water with me; a full bucket gives the body something honest to do.
Ruth Hale: Start the old tune at Independence Rock. By the second line, even the homesick will be singing into their sleeves.
Ruth Hale: I warm a sick child's hands between mine before I offer broth; cold fingers refuse comfort.
Ruth Hale: Open the sleeping tent a while after fever. Rain may come, but stale air is no medicine.
Ruth Hale: I have learned that a cup of water offered without advice is sometimes the best nursing.
Ruth Hale: One linen scrap from each family, please. After sickness arrives, every scrap has already found a purpose.
Ruth Hale: I sing low beside the fire when snow closes the road, because frightened people hear a loud song as a lie.
Ruth Hale: Leave that coffee cup dull. The last clean rag belongs on the fevered brow.
Ruth Hale: I tell a weary mother to sleep first and apologize later; exhaustion makes small sorrows sound like judgments.
Ruth Hale: Give me his full name for my list. The road may forget it after Fort Boise; we will not.
Ruth Hale: I ask the well ones to fetch wood for the sick; care is easier to bear when it is shared.
Ruth Hale: Here is peppermint for your stomach. Sit by me until the worry passes; you need not explain it.
Ruth Hale: I keep children busy gathering smooth stones for a grave; their hands need work when words fail.
Ruth Hale: I cannot promise an easy tomorrow. I can promise we will make breakfast if we have breath and flour.
Ruth Hale: I lace a cold person's boots loosely at night, so swollen feet have room to rest.
Micah Reed: The shirt around my hammer was my brother's. The cloth is worn through, but I have not changed it.
Micah Reed: I heat a bent tire slowly and cool it slow, or the iron remembers the crack.
Micah Reed: Both wheels are shaking. Spend a day at my fire now, or spend three days beside the road later.
Micah Reed: I save every bent nail in a tin; straightening iron is easier than finding it past Fort Hall.
Micah Reed: Quiet a moment. That chain is loose. Metal confesses plainly when the camp quits talking over it.
Micah Reed: I set a broken trace with rivets, not hope; hope may travel with us, but it will not pull an ox.
Micah Reed: My cold chisel rides under my coat in rain. Rust starts its work before the wet leaves your hands.
Micah Reed: I mend pots for hungry families first; a cracked skillet turns good flour into a poor supper.
Micah Reed: After my brother died, I hammered until dawn. The empty tent was louder when I stopped.
Micah Reed: I put a new ring on a wheel before a mountain descent; that is not a place for borrowed iron.
Micah Reed: Pump the bellows slow, child. The fire has rules, but it will teach you if you listen.
Micah Reed: I pay for good charcoal when I have coin; green wood smoke makes weak iron and weaker tempers.
Micah Reed: My file lives in a boot leg. A dull blade turns a small repair into night work, and we are late enough.
Micah Reed: I have patched a wagon with barrel hoops, mule shoes, and one prayer; the prayer was the weakest part.
Micah Reed: One cup at a time on that axle. Pour the whole bucket and you may split metal clean through.
Micah Reed: I sharpen the hunting knife before dawn, not when the deer is down and every hand wants it.
Micah Reed: A widow asked for a new latch, so she has one. A wagon door ought to close against wind and worry.
Micah Reed: I hang my tools in the same order each night, so I know what is missing before the train rolls.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Silas Enright: Rest the oxen a spell before you push on.
speakers.name: Silas Enright
speakers.returning_greeting: Silas Enright: Back at my gate again. Good.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Delia Marsh: Fort Laramie welcomes every wagon that reaches it whole.
speakers.name: Delia Marsh
speakers.returning_greeting: Delia Marsh: You made it back to my counter.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Amos Truett: Mountain men know this pass better than any map.
speakers.name: Amos Truett
speakers.returning_greeting: Amos Truett: Still standing, I see.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Verity Combs: The Snake River road is dry this time of year.
speakers.name: Verity Combs
speakers.returning_greeting: Verity Combs: You've the look of a wagon I've met before.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Reuben Slate: Not many wagons stop twice at my post.
speakers.name: Reuben Slate
speakers.returning_greeting: Reuben Slate: Twice now. I remember faces.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Content Ashby: The Dalles is close now; mind the last grade.
speakers.name: Content Ashby
speakers.returning_greeting: Content Ashby: Good to see a familiar wagon.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Osric Vane: California wagons keep to the south road from here.
speakers.name: Osric Vane
speakers.returning_greeting: Osric Vane: You again. Keep to the south road, I said.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Prudence Oakes: Every wagon asks the same questions here.
speakers.name: Prudence Oakes
speakers.returning_greeting: Prudence Oakes: Back with the same good sense as before.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Barnabas Cutter: The Humboldt road is long; carry water enough.
speakers.name: Barnabas Cutter
speakers.returning_greeting: Barnabas Cutter: Made it back to me. Fair going.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Honor Ridley: Mormon families rest here before South Pass.
speakers.name: Honor Ridley
speakers.returning_greeting: Honor Ridley: A returning face is a welcome one.

speakers.favor_text: a sack of cornmeal for the road
speakers.greeting: Calvert Nash: The Hastings road saves miles but not always time.
speakers.name: Calvert Nash
speakers.returning_greeting: Calvert Nash: You took my advice and came back to tell it.
